title: Asada wants stronger household demand before the next rate rise
summary: Bank of Japan Policy Board member Toichiro Asada would look for stronger evidence that higher wages were generating household demand and, through that demand, sustained price increases before supporting another rate rise. In Nagasaki on 12 November he explained his dissents from the June and September hikes, which had taken the policy rate to 1.25%, and his votes for no change in July and October. The October Outlook Report retained the Board’s case for further tightening as conditions warranted. Asada accepted the risk of inflation overshooting. His concern was the growing cost of acting before the effects of earlier decisions could be observed (pp. 4–7).

The clearest tension was between the labour market and what households were buying. Unemployment was around 2.5%, scheduled cash earnings were growing at roughly 3% year on year, summer bonuses were up and real wages had been rising year on year since the start of 2026. Yet private consumption was almost flat in the April–June GDP accounts. Asada acknowledged institutional influences on that quarter, but saw little momentum in the Bank’s Consumption Activity Index either. Chart 6 separates services, durables and non-durables in the cumulative change since early 2022. A recovery over that whole period could coexist with a recent plateau. AI-related demand for Japanese IT and capital goods, high corporate profits and investment plans supported aggregate activity without establishing a household-led expansion (pp. 1–2, Charts 2–6).

The inflation measures answered different questions. Recent annual CPI inflation excluding fresh food was about 2%. Excluding fresh food and energy gave around 2.5%. A third measure excluding fresh food and institutional influences, including government energy relief and free education, gave 3.0–3.5%. The last figure removes policies that materially affect the prices households pay. A weaker yen and more expensive imported commodities raised input costs, with the speed of pass-through still uncertain. The October Board forecast put fiscal-year CPI inflation excluding fresh food at 2.5% in 2026, 2.6% in 2027 and 2.0% in 2028. Those are medians of members’ forecasts. Underlying inflation was judged broadly consistent with the target, and medium- to long-term expectations were around 2% (pp. 2–5, Charts 7–8, 11–12).

Financing conditions explain why the same size of rate increase might matter more now. Lending rates and issuance yields on commercial paper and corporate bonds had risen. Short real rates remained negative, longer real rates appeared to have turned positive, and firms’ assessments of their financial positions had shown little deterioration. The real rates in Chart 10 are estimates using bond yields and maturity-matched inflation expectations. Asada thought it could take a year or more for a hike’s effect on firms and households to become clear. At 1.25% the policy rate already lay within the Bank’s wide estimate of nominal neutral, from just above 1% to 2.5%. Weak consumption could therefore translate a further hike into lower underlying inflation, even while import costs were lifting measured prices (pp. 5–7, Charts 9–10).

Asada separately described the October decision to accelerate sales of the Bank’s exchange-traded funds. Since sales began in January, they had proceeded smoothly and equity turnover had grown. The annual pace rose from ¥330bn to ¥860bn, taking the estimated disposal period from 112 years to roughly 43. The Bank retained discretion to adjust or suspend sales temporarily in response to market conditions. This decision concerned the execution of a long disposal programme. Asada attached no equity-price target or timetable for the next policy-rate decision to it (p. 8).

questions.question: Is the wage gain beginning to generate demand strong enough to change Asada’s vote?
questions.detail: The speech establishes gains in real earnings alongside nearly flat recent consumption. It leaves open whether the delay reflects a temporary distortion or households’ reluctance to spend additional income. The distinction matters for the timing of any policy-rate repricing. Compare subsequent Cabinet Office consumption estimates, the Bank’s Consumption Activity Index by component, and monthly earnings releases. Look for volume growth across categories after adjusting for the differences in coverage highlighted in Chart 6.

questions.question: How much of the next increase in CPI would survive the energy shock and changes to government relief?
questions.detail: The Board expected above-target CPI excluding fresh food in the near term. Asada questioned how far import costs would feed into underlying inflation. A persistent rise in domestic services prices with firmer demand would carry different implications for Japanese rates from an energy-driven jump. Use the component contributions and policy adjustments in Chart 8, the Statistics Bureau’s subsequent CPI breakdowns and the Bank’s underlying-inflation indicators to track the sources of the change.

questions.question: Where would the cumulative tightening appear before the aggregate financing survey deteriorates?
questions.detail: Asada observed rising borrowing costs and still-favourable financing assessments. The speech gives no distribution of debt reset dates or estimates of household sensitivity. These exposures matter for domestic credit risk and the plausible room for another hike. Compare the Tankan financing indicators by firm size with bank lending-rate releases, financial statements showing interest expense, and available mortgage reset data. Align those observations with the dates of the June and September increases.
